title: Fix the Mind, Not the Move: Interpretable AI Assistance via Knowledge-Gap Localization
one_liner: Infer which idea a user misunderstands, then give the smallest correction that removes that misunderstanding instead of only correcting the visible action.
lead: This paper argues that helpful assistance should target the cause of repeated mistakes, not only the latest bad move. SENSEI watches a user's actions, infers which part of the user's internal task knowledge is wrong or missing, and then gives a focused suggestion that repairs that knowledge gap because fixing the source should improve many later decisions, not just one step.

paras: Many assistants react to the latest mistake by telling the user what action to take next. That can prevent immediate failure, but it often does not improve the user's next attempt because the underlying belief that caused the mistake is still wrong. The user may repeat the same pattern in a slightly different form.

The paper treats human errors as evidence about hidden knowledge gaps. If the assistant can locate the mistaken concept, it can offer a smaller and more useful correction because the advice addresses the reason the mistake happened.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Map observed behavior back to a structured task-knowledge graph, locate the missing or wrong concept, and intervene at that concept.

panels.title: 1. User makes a wrong move
panels.viz_args: Observed action is wrong, but the cause is not visible
panels.caption: A bad action is only the surface signal.

panels.title: 2. Many hidden misconceptions could cause it
panels.caption: One behavior can come from several different misunderstandings.

panels.title: 3. SENSEI localizes the gap
panels.viz_args: Trace behavior against a task knowledge structure
panels.caption: The system asks which missing concept best explains the observed pattern.

panels.title: 4. Give the smallest sufficient correction
panels.viz_args: Explain only the concept that unlocks correct later actions
panels.caption: The advice is narrow because broad advice adds clutter without fixing the core issue.

panels.title: 5. Later choices improve
panels.caption: Performance improves across the task because the user now reasons from a better internal picture.

steps.b: Represent the task as structured knowledge
steps.text: Store the concepts, dependencies, and rules that a user needs in order to act correctly.
Collect the sequence of decisions and outcomes so that behavior can be matched to possible misconceptions.
Find which wrong or missing concept best explains the pattern of mistakes.
Offer the smallest explanation that repairs the gap because targeted advice is easier to absorb and reuse.
Measure whether later task choices improve so that the system can tell whether the intervention worked.

paras: The paper changes the target of assistance. Instead of only changing the next action, it changes the user's internal task knowledge.

hidden.name: Knowledge gap location
paras: The key hidden quantity is which concept in the user's task knowledge is wrong, missing, or improperly linked. You cannot observe that gap directly. You only see actions, delays, or repeated failures.

SENSEI treats those visible behaviors as clues. It looks for the smallest concept-level explanation that accounts for the pattern because that produces a correction that is specific enough to help without overwhelming the user.

heat.caption: Darker means the system considers that concept a stronger explanation for the observed mistakes.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the mistaken idea in the user's head.
The method localizes a misconception inside a structured task representation so that assistance is concept-level rather than action-level.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: correct the cause, not only the symptom
paras: A repeated behavioral pattern usually comes from a repeated internal mistake. If the assistant only patches the last action, the user may still generate the same error later because the decision rule that produced it has not changed. A concept-level intervention has longer reach because many later actions depend on the same underlying concept.

The paper also stresses minimality. A small correction helps because it reduces the chance that the assistant distracts the user with extra information. When the system identifies the narrowest gap that explains the failure, it can supply just enough guidance to repair the user's decision process.

stages.s: User actions over a long task
Match behavior to possible concept gaps

math.words: A simple view is to choose the misconception that best explains the observed mistakes while keeping the correction small. The system prefers a gap if that gap predicts the user's behavior well and requires little extra explanation.
symbols: overall value of treating a given concept gap as the cause
how well that gap accounts for the observed user actions
how much extra instruction is needed to repair that gap

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the user repeatedly performs step C before step B.
Gap 1: missing ordering rule. Explanation score 9, advice cost 2, total 7.
Gap 2: wrong goal concept. Explanation score 6, advice cost 4, total 2.
Gap 3: tool misuse. Explanation score 5, advice cost 3, total 2.
The system picks the ordering rule because it explains the pattern best and needs the least extra instruction.

math.note: The paper uses structured reasoning over knowledge components rather than this exact formula, but the formula captures the tradeoff between explanatory power and intervention size.

charts.title: Action-level correction only
charts.note: Surface corrections help immediately, but later performance stays weak because the underlying misunderstanding remains in place.

charts.title: Knowledge-gap localization
charts.note: Targeted concept repair works better because it changes the reason the user was making the mistake. The values are illustrative summaries of the reported trend.

items.b: The knowledge structure may be incomplete.
items.html: If the task representation misses an important concept, the system can only guess among the concepts it knows, so localization may be wrong because the true cause is absent.
Two misconceptions may produce the same visible behavior, which makes correct localization hard unless the system has enough context to separate them.

items.b: Minimal advice can be too small.
items.html: A very short correction may fail if the user needs an example, a prerequisite reminder, or a more direct explanation before the new concept can be applied.
The paper is useful because it treats user support as diagnosis plus intervention, not only error prevention at the last step.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a structured task with ten concepts and explicit dependency links. Create users with planted misconceptions, including cases with two overlapping gaps. Let the users act in a long task so that behavior traces are recorded. Compare two helpers: one that only tells the next correct action, and one that localizes the concept gap and gives a focused explanation.

The demo should show higher later-task success for the localization system because repairing the concept should improve more than one step. Log both the predicted gap and the final advice so that a human can inspect whether the diagnosis made sense.
demo.closing: The demo must prove that concept-level help improves long-run behavior because it fixes the source of repeated mistakes.
